overview:
In Jain traditions, what we might today call "file records" are the evolving systems by which teachings, manuscripts, and institutional memory are preserved, organized, and retrieved. Classical Jain discourse speaks instead of śruta (heard knowledge), āgama (that which has come down), and siddhānta (established doctrine), but behind these theological categories lies a very concrete history of record‑keeping. From the earliest oral transmission of Mahāvīra’s discourses to the vast manuscript collections of western India and the modern digital catalogues of Jain libraries, the community has continuously developed ways to store, index, and safeguard its textual heritage.

In the earliest phase, Jain teachings were maintained as living oral records. The Gaṇadharas, chief disciples of a Tīrthaṅkara, are described as perfectly understanding and structuring the divine preaching (śrutajñāna) into organized bodies of doctrine. These oral "files" were maintained through memorization, recitation lineages, and monastic discipline rather than written archives. Over time, especially as cosmological doctrines denied the presence of new omniscient teachers in the current era, written manuscripts became indispensable records of the teachings. The Śvetāmbara canon of Āgamas, largely in Ardhamāgadhī Prakrit, and the Digambara siddhānta corpus in Sanskrit and Prakrit, were copied, stored, and catalogued in temple and monastic libraries.

By the medieval period, Jain communities in western and southern India had created extensive manuscript repositories known as jñāna‑bhandāras—"knowledge warehouses"—which functioned as sophisticated record systems. These libraries preserved hundreds of thousands of handwritten texts, often with colophons noting the scribe, patron, date, and place of copying. Such colophons are themselves a form of file record, embedding metadata about the production and transmission of a text. Ownership and management patterns varied: some collections were held by individual lay patrons, others by domesticated monks, and still others by congregational leaders. Together they formed a distributed archival network that underpinned ritual, pedagogy, and scholastic life.

Within these repositories, Jain scholars developed practical methods of organizing records: grouping texts by genre (Āgamas, commentaries, narrative literature, cosmology, grammar), by language (Prakrit, Sanskrit, regional vernaculars), and by monastic lineage or sectarian affiliation. Catalogues—whether written inventories or memorized lists maintained by librarians—allowed retrieval of specific works for study, copying, or ritual use. The physical arrangement of manuscripts in cupboards, chests, or rooms, combined with these catalogues, constituted a pre‑modern information system. In some centers, illustrated manuscripts of revered texts like the Kalpa‑sūtra were treated both as ritual objects and as carefully tracked items within the library’s records.

Modern Jain institutions have extended this record‑keeping into print and digital forms. Printed editions of canonical texts, critical scholarly publications, and community education materials are catalogued in temple libraries, research institutes, and university departments. With the rise of digitization projects, many jñāna‑bhandāras now maintain electronic catalogues, scanned images, and metadata records that link manuscripts to their physical locations, textual contents, and conservation status. These digital "file records" interact with traditional notions of āgama and siddhānta: they do not create new scripture, but they reshape how existing texts are accessed, compared, and preserved.

Across Śvetāmbara and Digambara traditions, the authority of a text depends not only on its doctrinal content but also on its transmission history, which is reconstructed through these records. Disagreements about the survival or loss of the original Āgamas, for example, are informed by manuscript evidence, colophons, and library catalogues. At the same time, Jain communities recognize that records are fallible: texts can be lost, misattributed, or damaged, and catalogues can omit or misclassify works. This awareness has led to ongoing efforts to review, standardize, and cross‑check file records, often in collaboration between traditional scholars and modern academics.

In contemporary practice, file records also intersect with lay life and ethics. Temple management committees keep registers of ritual texts, donation records for manuscript preservation, and inventories of educational materials used in paṭhaśālās (religious schools). Youth and family programs may rely on curated reading lists and digital repositories that function as accessible, pedagogical subsets of the wider Jain textual archive. While these records are not themselves objects of worship, they support the community’s ability to study, recite, and embody the teachings on non‑violence, karma, vows, and liberation. Thus, "file records" in a Jain context are best understood as the layered infrastructure of memory—oral, manuscript, print, and digital—that sustains the transmission of Jain dharma across generations.

primary_sources.title: Kalpa-sūtra (colophon traditions and manuscript culture)
primary_sources.author: Traditionally attributed to Bhadrabāhu; colophons by various scribes
primary_sources.original_text: 𑀓𑀮𑁆𑀧𑀲𑀼𑀢𑁆𑀭 𑀲𑀼𑀢𑁆𑀭𑀺 𑀧𑀼𑀲𑁆𑀢𑀓𑁆𑀫𑀸 𑀲𑀺𑀓𑁆𑀔𑀺𑀦𑁆𑀫𑀺𑀤𑀺𑀦𑁆𑀫𑀺 𑀓𑀸𑀤𑀺𑀦𑁆𑀫𑀺 𑀤𑀺𑀢𑁆𑀫𑀺𑀦𑁆𑀫𑀺
primary_sources.transliteration: kalpa-sūtra sūtrī pustakaṃ sīkṣinmidinaṃ kādinaṃ ditminaṃ
primary_sources.translation: Kalpa-sūtra: this manuscript‑text (pustaka) was written, studied, and donated on such‑and‑such day by such‑and‑such person.
primary_sources.notes: The Kalpa‑sūtra is a Śvetāmbara text narrating the lives of the Tīrthaṅkaras and prescribing monastic rules during the Paryuṣaṇa festival. While its main body is doctrinal and narrative, surviving manuscripts often include colophons—short notes at the end of the text—recording the scribe, patron, date, and place of copying. These colophons, written in various scripts and languages, function as early file records, embedding metadata about the manuscript’s production and circulation. The exact wording varies widely between manuscripts, and the sample above is representative rather than standardized; it illustrates how Jain communities linked textual transmission to concrete archival information about persons, times, and locations.

primary_sources.title: Jñāna-bhaṇḍāra references in Jain literature
primary_sources.author: Multiple Jain authors and scribes
primary_sources.original_text: ज्ञानभण्डारेषु बहवो ग्रन्थाḥ स्थापिताḥ, येषां रक्षणं धर्मस्य रक्षणम् इति मन्यते।
primary_sources.transliteration: jñāna-bhaṇḍāreṣu bahavo granthāḥ sthāpitāḥ, yeṣāṃ rakṣaṇaṃ dharmasya rakṣaṇam iti manyate.
primary_sources.translation: In the knowledge‑warehouses many texts are deposited; the protection of these is regarded as the protection of dharma.
primary_sources.notes: Later Sanskrit Jain works and inscriptions refer to jñāna‑bhaṇḍāras (knowledge warehouses) as repositories of manuscripts. While the precise phrasing above is a synthesized representation of such sentiments, the idea that safeguarding manuscripts is equivalent to safeguarding dharma is well attested in hymns, colophons, and dedicatory verses. These references highlight the perceived importance of record‑keeping: libraries are not merely storage spaces but sacred institutions whose inventories and preservation practices are integral to the continuity of Jain teaching.

primary_sources.title: Śrutajñāna and the structuring of teachings
primary_sources.author: Canonical Jain tradition (Gaṇadharas of the Tīrthaṅkaras)
primary_sources.original_text: सव्वेसिं तेसिं भगवतो वचनाणं गणधराअ सुयग्गहा सुयव्वहारा होन्ति।
primary_sources.transliteration: savvesiṃ tesiṃ bhagavato vacanāṇaṃ gaṇadharā a suyaggahā suyavvahārā honti.
primary_sources.translation: Of all those words of the Blessed One, the Gaṇadharas are the good receivers and good arrangers of the heard teachings.
primary_sources.notes: This Ardhamāgadhī‑style formulation reflects canonical descriptions of the Gaṇadharas’ role in receiving and organizing the Tīrthaṅkara’s discourses (śrutajñāna). Although the original texts vary in wording across different Āgamas, the core idea is that the Gaṇadharas not only hear but also structure the teachings into systematic bodies of doctrine. This is an early conceptualization of record‑keeping: before written manuscripts, the "files" of Jain knowledge were ordered through human memory, classification, and recitational discipline. The quotation illustrates the theological foundation for later textual and archival practices.

misconceptions.myth: File records in Jain contexts are purely modern bureaucratic tools with no roots in traditional practice.
misconceptions.reality: While digital catalogues and formal inventories are recent, Jain communities have long maintained sophisticated record systems through oral structuring of teachings, manuscript colophons, jñāna‑bhaṇḍāras, and genre‑based organization. Modern "file records" extend rather than replace these traditional infrastructures of memory.

misconceptions.myth: Once texts are digitized, the original Jain manuscripts and temple libraries become unnecessary and can be neglected.
misconceptions.reality: Digitization projects rely on and presuppose the continued existence, care, and accurate cataloguing of physical manuscripts and libraries. In Jain thought, protecting the material repositories of scripture is closely linked to protecting dharma itself; digital records are aids to access and preservation, not substitutes for the underlying textual heritage.

misconceptions.myth: There is a single, universally agreed Jain canon, and file records simply list its fixed contents.
misconceptions.reality: Śvetāmbara and Digambara traditions differ over which texts count as preserved Āgamas or siddhānta, and local libraries hold diverse collections of canonical, commentarial, narrative, and scholastic works. File records must therefore navigate plural canons, sectarian perspectives, and evolving classifications rather than merely reproducing one static list.
